research.job_description_summary: TCS hires fresh graduates (B.E./B.Tech., M.E./M.Tech., MCA, M.Sc./M.S.) through one integrated National Qualifier Test (NQT) held on TCS iON. Part A (Foundation, 75 min) covers numerical, verbal and reasoning ability; Part B (Advanced, 115 min) covers advanced quantitative and reasoning ability and 90 minutes of advanced coding. Performance in the test routes candidates to the Prime, Digital or Ninja track (listed fresher CTC: Prime 9.0 LPA, Digital 7.0 LPA, Ninja 3.36 LPA for UG), followed by interviews.
required_skills: Advanced coding in C, C++, Java, Python or C#
limitations: The official TCS NQT page lists the test structure and CTC but names no job roles, no interview rounds and no 2026 dates; interview-round details come from secondary sources and candidate reports.
Sources disagree on whether Ninja candidates face a coding section and on whether the coding section has 2 or 3 problems; coding rounds are therefore labeled REPORTED, not DOCUMENTED.

Candidate reports are anonymous public summaries (careerforfreshers.com, prepinsta.com) and cannot be independently verified; they are marked UNVERIFIED. Report months (April to August 2026) come from the source text, but the article publication dates are not shown.
The 'real questions' lists on jobrise.io and hirist.tech cite no candidate reports, so they were used only as topic context, not as evidence that TCS asked a question.
Several items come from a 2023 GeeksforGeeks Digital-track report and are labeled low confidence.
Ninja, Digital and Prime are hiring tracks, not official job titles; the title Assistant System Engineer comes from a candidate report.
Aptitude MCQs and the two Prime coding problems marked D are original practice items, not reported questions.
Cutoff percentiles and track-wise round counts quoted by secondary guides are unofficial and were not used as facts.
Evidence from other tracks: a few questions rest on reports from a different TCS track or on a 2023 report; they are marked NEEDS_REVIEW or low confidence and noted in each question.

Coverage gaps: aptitude has only a handful of practice items against a much larger real test; graphs, trees, dynamic programming and system design are not covered because no 2026 report in the sources mentions them for freshers.

questions.subtopic: Longest substring with at most K distinct characters
questions.prompt: Given a string and an integer k, find the length of the longest substring that contains at most k distinct characters.
questions.relevance_to_role: An older (2023) Digital-track report included a K-distinct-characters substring problem; sliding-window reasoning matches the Prime coding bar.
questions.expected_answer: Expand the right pointer; while the window has more than k distinct characters, shrink from the left.
follow_ups: How would you return the substring itself?
common_mistakes: Not removing zero-count entries when shrinking
questions.notes: Source is a 2023 report; low confidence. Wording and limits are original, and 'at most k' is used instead of the reported exact phrasing. Track unconfirmed: the evidence is a 2023 Digital-track report, not a Prime report.

coding.problem_statement: Given a string s and an integer k, print the length of the longest substring of s that has at most k distinct characters.
edge_cases: k larger than distinct characters in s
coding.expected_algorithm: Sliding window with a frequency map.

questions.prompt: Remove repeated words from a sentence, keeping the first occurrence of each word.
questions.relevance_to_role: Reported in a May 2026 Prime-track account; checks hashing and tokenization.
questions.expected_answer: Iterate through words; output a word only if it has not been seen.
common_mistakes: Sorting and losing the original order
Splitting on a single space only

coding.problem_statement: Given a sentence, print it with every repeated word removed, keeping the first occurrence of each word in order. Matching is case-sensitive.
coding.input_format: One line: words separated by single spaces.

samples.input: to be or not to be

edge_cases: Different cases of the same word
coding.expected_algorithm: Split into words and keep a hash set of words already seen.

questions.prompt: Merge all overlapping intervals into the smallest set of non-overlapping intervals. Intervals that touch at an endpoint are considered overlapping.
questions.relevance_to_role: Original Prime-level practice problem; sorting plus a linear sweep is typical of the advanced coding section.
questions.expected_answer: Sort by start, then merge when the next start <= current end.
follow_ups: How would you insert one new interval into an already merged list?
common_mistakes: Using < instead of <= for touching intervals
questions.notes: Original practice question; samples verified by running a reference solution.

coding.problem_statement: Given n closed intervals [l, r], print the merged non-overlapping intervals sorted by start. Intervals that share an endpoint are merged.
coding.input_format: Line 1: n. Next n lines: l and r.
coding.output_format: One merged interval per line as 'l r'.
coding.expected_algorithm: Sort by start and sweep, extending the current interval.

questions.prompt: Count the contiguous subarrays whose elements add up to exactly k. The array may contain negative numbers.
questions.relevance_to_role: Original Prime-level practice problem on prefix sums; negative values rule out a simple sliding window.
questions.expected_answer: For each prefix sum, add the count of earlier prefixes equal to prefix - k.
follow_ups: Why does a sliding window fail here?
questions.notes: Original practice question; samples verified by running a reference solution.

coding.problem_statement: Given an array of n integers and an integer k, print the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals k.
coding.input_format: Line 1: n and k. Line 2: n integers.
coding.expected_algorithm: Prefix sums with a hash map of prefix frequencies.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a JSON Web Token and how a server verifies one.
questions.relevance_to_role: JWT structure was asked in a May 2026 Prime-track account.
questions.expected_answer: A JWT has three Base64URL-encoded parts: header (algorithm, type), payload (claims such as subject and expiry) and signature. The signature is computed over header.payload with a secret (HMAC) or private key (RSA/ECDSA). The server recomputes or verifies the signature and checks exp, issuer and audience. The payload is encoded, not encrypted, so no secrets belong in it.
follow_ups: How do you revoke a JWT before it expires?

questions.prompt: Which SQL commands control a transaction, and what does write-ahead logging guarantee?
questions.relevance_to_role: Transaction commands and WAL appeared in a May 2026 Prime-track account.
questions.expected_answer: BEGIN or START TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT control a transaction, supporting ACID properties. With write-ahead logging, changes are recorded in a durable log before data pages are written, so after a crash the database can redo committed work and undo uncommitted work, giving durability and atomicity.
common_mistakes: Saying WAL stores only successful writes

questions.prompt: Sketch the architecture of a simple LLM-based agent that answers customer queries by calling internal tools. What are the main components and failure modes?
questions.relevance_to_role: An August 2026 Prime-track AI/ML account was asked to design an AI-agent architecture.
questions.expected_answer: Main parts: a language model as planner, a tool registry with typed schemas, state and memory (conversation plus retrieved knowledge), an orchestration loop (observe, decide, act), guardrails and logging. Failure modes: wrong or invented tool calls, loops, prompt injection, stale data, cost and latency. Mitigate with validation, step limits, evaluation sets and human escalation.
follow_ups: How would you test the agent before launch?
common_mistakes: Naming frameworks without explaining the loop
questions.notes: Reported by one candidate (August 2026); the report also mentioned a graph-based agent framework.

questions.prompt: Explain the bias-variance trade-off and how you recognise underfitting.
questions.relevance_to_role: Bias, variance and underfitting were part of a Prime-track AI/ML account in August 2026.
questions.expected_answer: High bias means the model is too simple and underfits: both training and validation errors are high. High variance means it overfits: low training error but high validation error. Balance with model capacity, regularization, more data and cross-validation.
follow_ups: How would a learning curve show underfitting?
common_mistakes: Saying more data always fixes underfitting

questions.prompt: How would you reduce hallucinations in an LLM application that answers questions from company documents?
questions.relevance_to_role: Hallucination and retrieval topics appeared in two 2026 AI/ML-track accounts.
questions.expected_answer: Use retrieval-augmented generation: chunk and embed documents, retrieve the most relevant passages (optionally re-ranked), and instruct the model to answer only from them with citations and to abstain when evidence is missing. Lower the temperature, evaluate with test questions, and add human review for high-risk answers.
follow_ups: How do you decide chunk size?
questions.notes: Reported in two accounts (July and August 2026).

questions.prompt: Which data structure would you use to let a user move forward and backward between open browser tabs, and what are the operation costs?
questions.relevance_to_role: An older (2023) TCS Digital report included this data-structure choice question.
questions.expected_answer: A doubly linked list lets you move to the next or previous node in O(1) and insert or remove at a known node in O(1). An array with a current index also works for navigation but makes middle insertions O(n).
follow_ups: How would you implement back/forward history?
common_mistakes: Choosing a singly linked list without noting backward cost
questions.notes: Source is a 2023 report; low confidence. Track unconfirmed: the evidence is a 2023 Digital-track report, not a Prime report.

questions.prompt: Give a real-world use for Dijkstra's algorithm and one for Floyd-Warshall, and explain when you would choose each.
questions.relevance_to_role: An older (2023) TCS Digital report asked for real-life uses of both algorithms.
questions.expected_answer: Dijkstra finds shortest paths from one source with non-negative weights in about O((V+E) log V), such as navigation. Floyd-Warshall finds all-pairs shortest paths in O(V^3) and tolerates negative edges without negative cycles, such as a precomputed distance table for a small network. Choose Dijkstra for a single source on large sparse graphs, Floyd-Warshall for small dense graphs needing all pairs.
follow_ups: What would you use if edges can be negative and you need a single source?
questions.notes: Source is a 2023 report; low confidence. Track unconfirmed: the evidence is a 2023 Digital-track report, not a Prime report.

questions.prompt: TCS may rotate you across technologies or locations, or place you in a different role than you hoped for. How would you respond?
questions.relevance_to_role: Rotational work, relocation and accepting a different role came up in two 2026 Prime/NQT accounts.
questions.expected_answer: A willing but honest answer, backed by a time you adapted to change.

rubric.criterion: Own actions and reasoning are clear

follow_ups: Which technology would you least like to work on, and how would you handle it?
common_mistakes: Saying yes to everything without any substance
questions.notes: Reported in two accounts; one report also mentioned an unspecified abbreviation (MCP) whose meaning the source did not give.

behavioral.star_guidance: Situation: a time you had to change plans or learn something new quickly. Action: how you adapted. Result: what you gained. Link it to your readiness here.
positive_signals: Shows openness with a real example

questions.prompt: Tell me about a student activity beyond academics where you took initiative, and what you gained from it.
questions.relevance_to_role: Student activities were discussed in a May 2026 Prime-track account.
questions.expected_answer: A specific activity where the candidate acted first, with a clear outcome and a lesson.

rubric.criterion: Own actions and reasoning are clear

follow_ups: How did you get others to join?

behavioral.star_guidance: Situation: the activity or club. Task: the problem or goal. Action: what you started or led. Result: impact and learning.

questions.relevance_to_role: An older (2023) TCS Digital report included this question; confidence is lower.
questions.expected_answer: A concrete challenge, how it was approached, and the resulting growth.

rubric.criterion: Own actions and reasoning are clear

follow_ups: What did you do to prepare?
common_mistakes: Choosing an example with no real challenge
